title: Simple deductive proof

points.text: Setting out a proof from the left-hand side to the right-hand side; equals versus identity symbols

bigPicture: A proof shows a statement is true for every case, not just the ones you tried. AA SL proofs are short: write the general case in algebra and transform one side into the other.

keyIdeas.cue: What is a deductive proof, and how do you write general numbers?
keyIdeas.answer: A chain of logical steps from definitions or known facts to the result, valid for every case. Examples never prove a general claim; one counterexample disproves it. Even: 2n; odd: 2n + 1; consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you set out a proof that LHS = RHS?
keyIdeas.answer: Start with one side (usually the more complicated), transform it step by step until it equals the other side, then write a conclusion. Don't work on both sides at once or start from what you want to prove. ≡ means identically equal (true for all values); = in an equation is true only for particular values.

keyTerms.def: true for every value of the variable; symbol ≡
one case that shows a general claim is false

workedExamples.title: Three consecutive integers
workedExamples.prompt: Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.
workedExamples.answer: a multiple of 3, so divisible by 3

misconceptions.right: Examples only illustrate; algebra for a general n proves it.

misconceptions.wrong: Writing both sides and cancelling to 0 = 0
misconceptions.right: Work from one side to the other.

practice.prompt: Prove that the square of any odd number is one more than a multiple of 8.
solution: n(n + 1) is a product of consecutive integers, so it is even: n(n + 1) = 2k
commonErrors: Stopping at 4n(n + 1) + 1 without explaining why it is 8k + 1
Using the same letter for two different odd numbers

assessmentNote: AA SL external exams: Paper 1 without a calculator and Paper 2 with a GDC, both written answers in sections A (short) and B (extended); no multiple choice. Practice prompts here are original and are not predictions of exam questions.

memorise: Algebraic forms for even, odd and consecutive numbers
Layout: LHS = … = RHS, then a concluding sentence
